name: Shaving soap / cream

card.summary: Lubricating soaps, creams, foams and gels for razor shaving; the aim is less friction, but no trials test it.
card.aka: shaving foam, shaving gel, shave soap
card.note: Alcohol-based and aerosol products can dry skin or be flammable.

lead: Shaving soap and shaving cream are lubricating products worked into the beard before a razor pass. They soften and hydrate the hair and let the blade glide, which people use to get a smoother, closer shave with fewer nicks and less razor irritation, and to keep a clean jawline, neckline and cheek line. [1][2]

They come in several forms: hard soap pucks or sticks and tubed lather creams that are whipped into foam with a brush, brushless creams without soap, aerosol foams and gels. [1] Wikipedia reports that lather creams generally contain 20 to 30 percent soap (potassium or triethanolamine) with up to about 10 percent glycerine, emollients and foaming agents, and that a humectant keeps the lather moist. [1]

Shaving products have a long history, from a wood-alkali and animal-fat preparation in Sumer around 3000 BC to Barbasol in 1919 and pressurised foams from 1949. [1] Online, the traditional wet-shaving community, for example on Lemmy's c/wetshaving, discusses soaps, tinned creams and history of old brands such as Williams. [3][4][5] No clinical trial of shaving soap or cream for appearance outcomes was found.

chain: Lather hydrates and softens facial hair
Lubricating layer lets the razor glide
Closer shave with less irritation and fewer nicks
angle.text: A good lather means the razor meets softened hair on a lubricated surface, so the result is a cleaner, smoother face and sharper beard lines. Many users also say the brush and lather routine makes shaving a more controlled process.

paras: Lather creams and soaps rely on soap, which foams when worked with water. Brushless creams are oil-in-water emulsions with humectants and wetting agents and no soap, so they do not lather. Aerosol foams are diluted lather creams with up to about 10 percent hydrocarbon propellant, and gels use different surfactant systems. [1]

Wikipedia says shaving cream softens hair by lubrication and by hydrating it, a process that depends on pH. Products for electric razors, where swollen hair is unwanted, contain 50 to 80 percent alcohol to dry the skin and stiffen hairs. [1]

Until the early twentieth century men mostly used hard soap bars or sticks, followed by tubes of oil and soft soap. Frank Shields, a former MIT professor, developed the first shaving cream in 1919, sold as Barbasol and packed by hand in Indianapolis. [1]

Rise, introduced in 1949, was the first pressurised shaving cream, and by the 1960s the pressurised format held about two thirds of the American market. CFC propellants were banned in the late 1990s over ozone concerns and replaced by hydrocarbon mixtures such as propane and butane. [1] A Lemmy post in the wet-shaving community looks back at Williams' political shaving-soap advertising from the 1896 US election. [4]

Users describe lather as the step that determines how comfortable the razor pass is, which affects redness, nicks and how clean the neckline looks afterwards. [3] In wet-shaving circles, people ask for tinned creams and soaps as an alternative to plastic tubes and spray cans. [3] A T Nation forum user in a 2010 thread names a badger brush, shaving soap and a safety razor as their preference over cartridge razors. [6]
Wikipedia notes that products for electric shaving are alcohol-based, whereas lather products are aimed at blade shaving. [1]

Alcohol-heavy products dry the skin, and aerosol products contain flammable hydrocarbon propellants, offset in cream formulations by high water content. [1] No clinical studies of irritation or allergy from shaving soaps or creams specifically were found.
No studies found of shaving soaps or creams as appearance or skin interventions. Physics papers use shaving foam as a model colloid, which is not research on skin effects.

lore.intro: Soap-and-brush shaving is discussed mainly in wet-shaving communities, with occasional mentions on fitness forums, where it is presented as a more satisfying alternative to canned foam.

claims.claim: A brush, soap and safety razor beats cartridge razors and canned foam
claims.believers: A T Nation poster says they will not go back to Gillette or Schick after switching to a badger brush, shaving soap and a safety razor. [6] Wet-shaving members similarly look for tinned soaps and creams. [3]
claims.experts: No published trials compare soap-and-brush shaving with canned foam for irritation or closeness. Wikipedia describes the products' composition and lubrication function without ranking them. [1]

quick.overview:
Shaving soap and cream coat the beard and skin so a razor glides with less friction. They come as bars, tubed creams, aerosol foams and gels, and have existed in some form since ancient Sumer.

Reference works describe their purpose as softer hair and less irritation, but no clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: Soap or surfactant, glycerine and emollients hydrate and soften hair and form a lubricating lather or film between blade and skin.
quick.risks: Alcohol-rich products dry the skin; aerosol cans use flammable propellants. No studies of product-specific irritation were found.
